- Uptime: 99.95% is our standard for the hosted plan; we can discuss 99.9% as an option for dedicated/private deployments or as a negotiated term tied to committed capacity.
- Credits: we typically cap monthly credits at a percentage of the monthly invoice but can offer a higher cap for enterprise commitments; need legal to propose language.
- Response/escation: 1-hour response for P1s is achievable for enterprise support tiers; on-call escalation is available with a premium.
- Maintenance: standard policy is 48-hour notice for planned maintenance with predefined off-peak windows; we can discuss 72-hour notices for regulated customers.

Thanks Lauren / Claire — I reviewed the attached redlines and pulled out the SLA/support sections. High-level legal positions and suggested alternatives below (I’ve included sample clause language in the attached PDF).

1) Uptime measurement and objective
- Legal concern: need precise definition of "Available" and measurement methodology (region vs. global, exclusion for scheduled maintenance, exclusion for customer-caused outages).
- Position A (preferred by Legal & Product): Keep 99.95% as baseline for hosted; if customer requires 99.9% instead, we can accept but add: (a) explicit exclusions for force majeure and customer misconfiguration, (b) measurement at the service-region-month level, and (c) a requirement that the customer use the Redwood monitoring agent/endpoint for incident correlation.
- Position B (compromise): Accept 99.9% in MSA, but include a contract addendum that defines remediation and longer notice for extended outages.

2) Service credits and caps
- Legal proposes a sliding credits table tied to monthly availability tiers with a maximum credit cap equal to 100% of the monthly recurring fees for the impacted service in a single month. We can offer a higher cap than standard for enterprise customers if finance approves.

3) Response times and escalation
- We can commit to 1-hour initial response for P1s on enterprise support; however, we need to ensure on-call escalation is limited to business hours unless the customer purchases 24x7 incident management.

4) Maintenance notice windows
- Operationally acceptable: 48–72 hours depending on change classification (critical vs. routine). For regulatory customers, we can agree to 72-hour notice plus a quarterly planned-maintenance calendar.

Action items: Neha to prepare tracked MSA redlines (SLA/support sections) by end of day Thursday 27 Aug; Marcus to confirm operational/metric definitions. Claire — please confirm whether Orion requires 24x7 on-call or business-hours escalation so we can align the language.

Regards,

Quick ops/engineering notes on feasibility and measurement:

- 99.95% vs 99.9%: For our multi-tenant hosted clusters, 99.95% is standard and achievable. Dropping to 99.9% lowers the bar, not raises it — I assume Orion asked for 99.9% (a lower figure) because of their risk appetite? Please confirm. For Dedicated/Private installs we can tune configs to hit either target with dedicated capacity and SLO monitoring.

- Measurement: We measure availability per-region per-calendar-month using our telemetry (uptime pings at 1m granularity + request success rates). We exclude scheduled maintenance windows (as defined in the contract) and customer-caused incidents (root-cause analysis required). I attached a short CSV that shows the metric fields we export.

- Maintenance windows: 72-hour notice for routine maintenance is fine for enterprise customers. For emergency patches, we need right-to-patch language with immediate notification and post-facto remediation reporting.

- Credits calculation: credits are computed on the impacted service SKU monthly invoice line. If Orion needs credits to apply across multiple SKUs, that requires finance approval; expect a decision timeline ~3 business days.

I can join the call to walk through the telemetry and explain how we compute downtime. Recommend we get Orion to accept our monitoring endpoint as the authoritative source (or accept mutually agreed third-party monitoring for arbitration).

Thanks,
Marcus Lin
